title: Maximum Sum of Almost Unique Subarray
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` and two positive integers `m` and `k`. A subarray (a contiguous, non-empty run of elements) is called **almost unique** when it holds at least `m` different values.

Among all almost unique subarrays of `nums` whose length is exactly `k`, return the largest element sum. If no subarray of length `k` is almost unique, return `0`.
signature: long maxSum(List<Integer> nums, int m, int k)
notes:
## Intuition

Every candidate has the same length `k`, so the candidates are the windows `nums[i..i+k-1]`. Checking each window from scratch (build a set, add up the values) costs O(n · k). Neighbouring windows share all but two elements: sliding one step right adds one value and drops one value. If we keep a running sum and a count of each value inside the window, both facts update in O(1) per step, and the number of distinct values is simply the number of keys with a non-zero count.

## Approach

1. Keep `count` (value to how many times it appears in the window), `windowSum` and `best = 0`.
2. For each `right`, add `incoming = nums[right]` to `count` and to `windowSum`.
3. Once `right >= k`, the window is one too long: remove `outgoing = nums[right - k]`, deleting its key when its count drops to 0, and subtract it from `windowSum`.
4. When the window is full (`right >= k - 1`) and `count.size >= m`, update `best` with `windowSum`.
5. Return `best`; it stays `0` when no window qualifies.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 6, 7, 3, 1, 7]`, `m = 3`, `k = 4`. At `right = 3` the window is `[2, 6, 7, 3]`: 4 distinct values, sum 18, so `best = 18`. At `right = 4`, 1 enters and 2 leaves: `[6, 7, 3, 1]`, 4 distinct, sum 17. At `right = 5`, 7 enters and 6 leaves: `[7, 3, 1, 7]`, 3 distinct (7 has count 2), sum 18. All three windows qualify and the largest sum is `18`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each element enters and leaves the window once, with O(1) map work.
- Space: O(k) for the counts of at most `k` values.

## Pitfalls

- Delete a value's key when its count reaches 0; otherwise `count.size` overcounts the distinct values.
- Only judge full windows: before `right = k - 1` the window is shorter than `k`.
- Sums reach `2 · 10^4 · 10^9 = 2 · 10^13`, beyond a 32-bit int, so use `long` in Java or C.
- Return `0`, not `-Infinity` or the smallest window sum, when no window has `m` distinct values.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | how many times each value appears in the current window |
| `windowSum` | sum of the current window |
| `best` | largest qualifying window sum so far |
| `right` | index of the newest element in the window |
| `incoming`, `outgoing` | the value entering and the value leaving the window |

narration.2: Map from value to how many times it occurs in the window; its size is the number of distinct values.
narration.3: Running sum of the elements currently in the window.
narration.4: Best qualifying sum so far; 0 is the answer if no window qualifies.
narration.6: Grow the window by one element on the right at each step.
narration.8: Count one more occurrence of it.
narration.9: Add it to the window's sum.
narration.11: Once right reaches k, the window holds k + 1 elements and must drop its leftmost one.
narration.12: The value leaving is k positions behind right.
narration.13: Count one fewer occurrence of it.
narration.14: If none of it remains in the window...
narration.15: ...remove the key so the map size stays equal to the number of distinct values.
narration.17: Take the leaving value out of the sum.
narration.20: The window is full and holds at least m distinct values, so it is almost unique.
narration.21: Keep the larger of the best so far and this window's sum.
narration.24: The largest almost unique window sum, or 0 if there was none.
